title: The true devotee
hook: titles mean nothing without the life that matches

segments.voice: Yesterday, pandit: the scholar who teaches his own mind first. Your line was teach your own mind. Today, ashtpadi nine turns to the devotee.

Someone volunteers at a shelter every Saturday, and makes sure to post a photo every time. Someone else drives an elderly neighbor to the doctor every month for years and never mentions it to anyone. Both did good. Photos aren't wicked. But only one of the two is plainly not waiting for anything back. Ashtpadi nine has two stanzas about devotees, and both land on exactly that point.
screen: `A PHOTO EVERY SATURDAY.` → `A NEIGHBOR DRIVEN FOR YEARS.` → `WHO WASN'T WAITING FOR ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: One stanza takes the title vaishnav, a devotee of Vishnu, an honored name. The true vaishnav, it says, is the one with whom God is well pleased, who lives apart from the pull of maya, the passing world. Then the striking line: karam karat hovai nihkaram. Doing deeds, he remains without deeds. Nihkaram means free of the deed, free of its grip. It doesn't mean doing nothing. It means doing the good thing without hooking yourself to the result. The next lines say it plainly: he doesn't hanker after the fruit of any action; he is absorbed only in devotion and the singing of praise. The next stanza takes another devotee's title, bhagauti, and says the same in a different key: the true one is dyed in love for God, leaves bad company behind, and every doubt dissolves from the mind. Two titles, one point. Devotion is measured by the life underneath it, and especially by whether it's waiting for a reward. The neighbor who drives someone to the doctor for years isn't keeping score. The deed is done; the doer isn't clinging. This isn't a criticism of the people who held these titles; the stanzas honor the names by asking them to be true. It's a mirror, held up to anyone who calls themselves devoted, in any community. Sikhs have a word for selfless service, seva, and its whole point is the same: the life, not the title.
screen: `VAISHNAV: AN HONORED NAME.` · `NIHKARAM: DOING, BUT NOT GRIPPED.` · `NO HANKERING FOR THE FRUIT.` · `BHAGAUTI: DYED IN LOVE.` · then, large: `THE LIFE, NOT THE TITLE.`

segments.voice: Choose one value you care about, kindness, honesty, patience, and picture one small act of it that no one will see, like wiping a shared table or leaving a good review for a stranger's small shop. Notice any little wish to be noticed, and let it go on the out-breath. Breathe in: the deed; breathe out: no reward.
Nihkaram, free of the deed. Doing deeds, yet free of them, hankering after no reward.
Your line: the life, not the title. The deed is done, and the doer isn't clinging. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond, and read these stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as describing devotion that seeks no reward.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nihkaram, free of the deed; in ashtpadi nine, doing good without clinging to the result.

trapdoor: what you thought: a devotee is someone with a devout title.

what a scholar hears: 'karam karat hovai nihkaram' echoes a wider Indic ideal of desireless action; ashtpadi nine places it inside the vaishnav stanza.

chat.says: If I do good things and never get thanked, what's the point?
options: Ashtpadi nine's true devotee does good without hankering for the fruit; the deed is enough.
None. Nihkaram means it's wiser to do nothing at all than to go unthanked.
The point is the reward later; the stanza promises thanks for every deed.
chat.meaning: Karam karat hovai nihkaram: doing deeds, yet free of them. The true devotee hankers after no fruit of any action.

nihkaram.meaning: free of the deed and its grip

maya.meaning: the pull of the passing world

bhagauti.meaning: a devotee's title, given new life in the stanza
